articles.summary: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous…

blocks.text: Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.”

The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit.

Once in the voltage room, Sandu says the managers confirmed the lines had been de-energised. In the first round, everything went as planned. Then, on the second test, while holding insulated tongs, he linked the cables. But this time, the lines were live.

The blast was immediate and catastrophic. In milliseconds, 400 volts and 12,000 amps hit Sandu’s face and across the right side of his body. “I went completely blind,” he says. When doctors received him in the Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, he says he was placed in an induced coma for five days.

Hospital records seen by the Guardian and Investigate Europe show that the arc flash electrocution had burned 12% of Sandu’s body, with second-degree burns to the face and neck, as well as third-degree burns across his right shoulder and fingers.

blocks.caption: Sandu in hospital Photograph: Investigate Europe

blocks.text: When Sandu woke from surgery in the intensive care unit a week later, his wife was at his bedside. He says his entire body felt like a “white-hot blister … It was so much pain. The human heart cannot comprehend it.”

Sandu says the regional director of Google, along with a representative from Dornan Engineering, an Irish company that oversaw his contractor, and his recruiter, came to visit. While he lay bandaged in the hospital bed, he says the Google director told him he was lucky to be alive.
To date, no company or contractor appears to have been found liable for the accident. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation in late October and found no wrongdoing.

A spokesperson for Dornan Engineering said it was “committed to maintaining safe working conditions, complying with applicable labour laws and continually learning to help prevent incidents like this from happening again”.

Sandu’s electrocution appears brutal and harrowing, but far from unique, according to a five-month investigation by Investigate Europe and the Guardian into conditions for migrant workers on datacentre sites across Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Europe is in the midst of a datacentre boom, the largest infrastructure surge the continent has seen in decades, with more than 2,300 datacentres rapidly altering the physical and energy landscape of Europe (at least 500 of them in the UK) and hundreds more under construction.
But unions say the push for tech sovereignty in Europe is becoming increasingly reliant on the exploitation of migrant workers.

blocks.caption: The Google datacentre in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium. Photograph: Amazing Aerial/Alamy

blocks.text: In dozens of interviews we found evidence of debilitating injuries, squalid living conditions, an unreported infectious outbreak, unpaid wages and exploitative employment practices.

In the UK, a general contractor died while working on a datacentre site last year, while another fatality was reported in 2024 at an electrical substation being built for a Microsoft datacentre. Serious accidents have also been recorded this year at projects in Italy, Sweden, Norway and Belgium, and exploitative labour practices have been found at projects around the world, including in Brazil.

On the outskirts of Gävle, a city two hours north of Stockholm, past timber-framed cottages and dense pine forests, lies a smooth road leading to one such site. The remote clearing is part of a 130-hectare, €3bn expansion plan begun in June 2024 to scale up Microsoft’s AI datacentre infrastructure.
One subcontractor at the site is the Irish-owned construction company BenBau. It is among 148 firms working under Collen Construction at the Gävle site, including 28 direct subcontractors.

For months, there has been a growing sense of outrage among Adrian*, 45, and his colleagues working for BenBau on the Microsoft site. They showed evidence of crowded living quarters – 24 people to a kitchen, 14 men to a single bathroom – and say they have reported vermin infestations, broken ventilation systems and lack of heating during the sub-zero Swedish winters, but the problems remain.

blocks.caption: One worker claims he contracted TB at the Microsoft datacentre construction site at Gävle in Sweden.  Photograph: investigate-europe.org

blocks.text: Such conditions can make the transmission of disease more likely. In February this year, one Romanian worker tested positive for active tuberculosis, medical records show. Shortly after, others living in the same shared housing showed similar symptoms. BenBau initially informed only a few men who shared close quarters with the infected worker and then told the men that testing was optional, according to workers. After the first worker who contracted the disease had left for hospital, Benbau moved another worker into his bedroom.
Freedom of information requests made to Sweden’s national work authorities and its Public Health Agency say no outbreak had been reported.

The living and working conditions form only part of the story. More than 30 workers have shown hundreds of payslips to the Guardian and Investigate Europe that appear to show some of them working up to 50 or 60 hours a week with no overtime pay and missed holiday pay. With many foreign workers unfamiliar with the laws, unions say inequity can arise quickly.

Days before publication of this investigation, the union Solidariska Byggare, representing the 70 Romanian workers at Microsoft’s site in Gävle, brokered a settlement with BenBau, which it says will give workers back pay and allow unions access to sites.

A spokesperson for BenBau said the company “takes all concerns regarding the welfare, health and safety of our people extremely seriously” and has “stringent procedures for reporting, investigating and addressing workplace concerns”.

Since 2021, Sweden’s Work Environment Authority (AV) has opened 50 cases into working conditions at datacentre sites involving Microsoft and a number of Irish firms, according to a freedom of information request.

Earlier this month, a contractor fell through a roof hatch while carrying out maintenance work on a ventilation system at the Microsoft site in Gävle, according to freedom of information request to AV.

blocks.caption: A union meeting at Gävle to announce a settlement between affected workers and one construction company. Photograph: Valeria Altariova

blocks.text: In October 2021, a forklift allegedly ran over the foot of a supervisor working for Collen at the site. The worker subsequently needed surgery. An incident report submitted by Collen to work authorities says that the wrong machine had been used, the driver had no formal certificate for it and the lift plan was incomplete. Still, it had been signed off. The Work Environment Authority saw no grounds to report the employer to prosecutors.

A spokesperson for Collen said: “We are committed to ensuring that every Collen site is a safe, healthy and respectful place to work, where everyone is treated with dignity and their fundamental human rights are protected. We expect the same throughout our supply chain and have zero tolerance for any conduct inconsistent with these principles.

“Our projects are subject to rigorous compliance with our own mandatory policies and procedures, our clients’ requirements, all applicable laws and regulations, and recognised industry standards in every jurisdiction in which we operate.”

blocks.caption: A pamphlet circulated at the union negotiation with BenBau at Gävle, Sweden, in September.  Photograph: Mei-Ling McNamara

blocks.text: A similar pattern is found throughout Europe, says James McCabe from Unite the Union, an Irish-UK group representing more than 1.2 million workers. “Everywhere we’ve encountered Irish datacentre contractors at tech-giant datacentre sites we’ve learned of lack of normal and meaningful union access … as well as serious concerns of labour crimes and exploitation of workers,” he says.

Johan Danielsson, a European parliament rapporteur in charge of regulating subcontracting chains, says: “If people let these big American multinationals come here and import their anti-union business models, then it becomes a problem. Because behind the fence they are abusing workers, and they don’t want anyone to know it.”

A spokesperson for Google said: “Our supplier code of conduct and contracts require all suppliers to comply with local labour laws and uphold safe, healthy working conditions. We maintain active dialogue with union leaders and trade groups, and are committed to providing transparent information about our workplace.”

A spokesperson for Microsoft said: “In our datacentre construction, we work with contractors and suppliers, with whom we set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining. To ensure our contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies, we have robust processes in place, including audits.”
* Names have been changed

This investigation is led by Investigate Europe, a cross-border team of investigative journalists: Lorenzo Buzzoni, Jan Daalder, Pascal Hansens, Ella Joyner, Chris Matthews, Nico Schmidt and Astri Thunold.

articles.title: British Council’s £197m debt should mostly be written off, MPs say
articles.summary:
Commons report calls on Foreign Office to bail out soft-power flagship reeling from job cuts and asset sales

Ministers should explore writing off

blocks.text: Ministers should explore writing off a crippling £197m loan to the British Council by converting as much of it as possible into “a grant or similar”, MPs have said.

The Commons public accounts committee said the government lacked a “positive vision” for the council, whose soft power value to the UK is put at £1bn a year. The MPs called on the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to set out what more it could do to support the council and its work.
Despite slashing a third of its headcount and selling off historical assets, the council’s future remains precarious because a £60m Covid-era FCDO loan on commercial terms has grown to £197m.

The loan was agreed by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government when the pandemic shuttered the council’s English teaching and exams business overseas. The loan was due to have been repaid this year but was restructured to be cleared over the next 15 years.

Even with a turnaround plan to reduce staffing by a further 25% as well as dispose of more assets and close operations in nine countries, the council forecasts it will not generate an operating surplus until 2029–30, according to the committee.

The report said: “The FCDO should write to us on what steps could be taken to offset the loan against the soft power value provided by the British Council and convert as much of the loan as possible into a grant or similar.”

British Council staff across Europe have staged widespread strikes and protests against the cuts. The planned further job losses will mean numbers will have almost halved since 2020, with more than 2,000 full-time equivalent posts lost since 2021.
The report called on the FCDO and the council “to work together to set out a positive vision for the future of the British Council that will build on its soft power value to the UK”.

“It seems to the public accounts committee that the future of the British Council is still precarious and both it and the FCDO need to carefully monitor the situation as partners so that the British Council can confidently demonstrate to the world that the UK values its work in providing soft power,” it said.
The committee said it recognised the council’s “inestimable value” and called for a “more collaborative tone” in relations between the FCDO and council, where there has been “a lack of trust”.

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the committee, said: “With the council seeking a leaner operation at a time of continuing precarity and obvious vulnerability for its finances, it needs the government’s help to continue its vital work, not to be simply pursued as a debtor. The FCDO says the British Council must adapt to survive. That may be true – but it will fail to do so without the government’s full-throated support.”

The council is an arm’s-length body of the FCDO as well as an established charity and a commercial organisation. It operates in just under 100 countries and claims a reach of more than 700 million people a year.

The majority of its income is from its teaching and exams business, while grant-in-aid from the FCDO accounts for about 15% of its annual revenue. The funding is used to support the council’s three charitable objectives: cultural relationships, the English language and education.

articles.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
articles.summary:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating…

blocks.text: Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

blocks.caption: Cora Bailey, who founded the charity Claw, has encountered illegal miners since 1991. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian

blocks.text: Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

blocks.caption: Miners working illegally near the defunct Durban Deep goldmine. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian

blocks.text: In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

blocks.caption: The remains of the Durban Deep goldmine, which is now an illegal mining flashpoint. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian

blocks.text: Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

blocks.caption: A drone view of a section of Wemmer Pan Road, which was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian

blocks.text: However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

blocks.caption: A drone view of a collapsed section of Wemmer Pan Road near Rosettenville in Johannesburg. Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, says the biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian

blocks.text: Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

articles.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
articles.summary:
Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have…

blocks.text: Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

articles.title: Men can also be victims of sexual violence, Supreme Court says
articles.summary: Men can also be victims of sexual violence, Supreme Court says

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 12:55pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that men can also be victims of sexual violence, underscoring that the law must protect all victims of abuse regardless of gender.

In a 17-page decision, the SC En Banc affirmed that while women have historically suffered sexual violence by men, the law must be adaptable to also recognize that men can also be victims of perpetrators.

“... While there must be recognition of the historical injustice women have suffered, the law, as well as its interpretation, must be resilient enough to provide equal protection to all victims and guard against stereotypes that all women are victims and all men are perpetrators. When laws are not gender-neutral, male victims suffer twice: once at the hands of their abuser and second through the judicial system,” it said.
The SC also pointed out that the context of rape must not be viewed only through the lens of gender, but, “more importantly, of power.”
Power, the High Court said, is determined through a variety of factors including age, socioeconomic stature, and education.

“At its core, rape is an issue of power—an imposition of someone's dominance to violate the bodily autonomy of another. This power imbalance can manifest in many ways such as through differences in gender, age, socioeconomic stature, professional authority, or education,” the SC said.
“In rape, the perpetrator uses this power imbalance to coerce or manipulate the victim into submitting to their will or to make it impossible for the victim to refuse their advances,” it added.

According to court records, a woman was found guilty of committing acts of lasciviousness against her 11-year-old nephew, when she ordered him to take off his clothes, lie on the bed, and engaged in sexual intercourse with the boy.
Psychological debriefing and supportive psychotherapy diagnosed the child with post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the sexual abuse.
Records said that while the child did not protest at first because “he felt curious about what would happen," after the incident, he felt ashamed and contemplated committing suicide.

The woman argued that the child consented to the sexual act, but the SC disagreed. The Court cited that, at the time of the incident, the age of sexual consent was 12 years old, and deemed that the child was legally incapable of giving consent.

“The age of sexual consent when the incident happened in 2018 was still 12 years old before it was raised to 16 years old with the passage of Republic Act No. 11648 in 2022. Thus, AAA280727, an 11-year-old child at the time of the incident, is deemed unable to give consent,” the SC said.
Passed in 2022, Republic Act No. 11648 raised the age of consent to 16 years old, and revised the wording that a rape may be committed "by a person who shall have carnal knowledge of another person."
In the decision, the SC noted that many countries have now adopted gender-neutral rape laws to protect everyone’s sexual autonomy from the harm of non-consensual penetrative sexual acts.

“[T]here must be recognition in our laws that sexual violence devastates equally regardless of how it was committed or, at the very least, a reevaluation of whether the historical justifications for the distinctions in our rape laws are still relevant—and, more importantly, fair,” the SC said.

The woman was found guilty of statutory acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code. She was sentenced to prison for nine to 16 years and ordered to pay P250,000 in civil indemnity and damages.
The decision was penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen and promulgated on February 4, 2026. —VAL, GMA News

News
Published October 30, 2026 12:36pm
Mayon Volcano erupts, Alert Level 3 raised — PHIVOLCS
The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) on Friday reported a moderately explosive eruption of Mayon Volcano in Albay, prompting the raising of Alert Level 3.
In its Mayon Volcano Eruption Notification No. 1, PHIVOLCS said the eruption started at 11:53 a.m. and was still ongoing as of its latest advisory.
The eruption initially generated a grayish plume that rose approximately 3,000 meters above the crater and drifted west-southwest.
In a separate Facebook post, PHIVOLCS announced that Alert Level 3 has been raised over Mayon Volcano, which means increased tendency towards a hazardous eruption.

October 30, 2026
Merz pushes for new free trade network

blocks.caption: The German chancellor has been calling for a new global free trade networkImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Merz has again called for a global network of countries with a commitment to free trade based on international rules.
His comments came while in South Korea on the final day of his four-day trip to Asia. He was speaking at the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul.
"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," he said.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions," Merz added.
The chancellor had made a similar call in Singapore and Japan.
"German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region," South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook said at Thursday's conference.

articles.title: Ex-DA chief Montemayor's indictment for cyberlibel not persecution --PPI
articles.summary: The Planters Products Inc. (PPI) said the indictment of former Agriculture secretary Leonardo Montemayor for cyberlibel is not a persecution.

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 12:20pm
The Planters Products Inc. (PPI) said the indictment of former Agriculture secretary Leonardo Montemayor for cyberlibel is not a persecution.

To recall, in May 2026, the PPI filed a cyberlibel case against Federation of Free Farmers chairperson Montemayor over his allegations that the company is a GOCC as he questioned PPI’s importation of about 22,750 metric tons of rice from Vietnam.
PPI has insisted that it is not a government-owned corporation and its shares of stocks are owned by private individuals and entities, not by the government whether directly or indirectly.
This month, Office of the City Prosecutor-Makati found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction for one count of cyberlibel and two counts of oral defamation against Montemayor.

Prosecutors, in particular, found that Montemayor's statements accusing PPI of "engaging in unfair competition against Filipino farmers" and portraying it as a government-owned or controlled corporation were defamatory and malicious.
Makati Regional Trial Court Branch 148 ordered Montemayor's arrest on October 26. He has since posted bail. His arraignment is scheduled for November 24.
In a statement, Atty. Czarina G. Quintanilla-Raz, PPI legal counsel and spokesperson, said the company would support prosecutors in presenting evidence and pursuing accountability through the courts.
Quintanilla-Raz also slammed the “portrayal of the case as persecution,” saying “the issue concerned truth and falsehood.”

This came after MAGSASAKA Party-list and the FFF said, “there is absolutely nothing libelous in stating this legal fact, nor is it defamatory to demand transparency and accountability from a government-controlled entity that has engaged in the massive, questionable importation of rice to the direct detriment of Filipino farmers.”

“With the recent string of arrests targeting critics and advocates who dare to question agricultural cartels and administrative overreach, it has become clear that defending the Filipino farmer is now a dangerous endeavor,” FFF and MAGSASAKA Party-list said.
Quintanilla-Raz, however, said that “making unfounded, defamatory accusations carries legal consequences, regardless of a person's former government position.”
"Freedom of expression does not give anyone the right to make defamatory statements or present unsupported allegations as established facts," she said.
Quintanilla-Raz reiterated that PPI is a private corporation, separate from the Department of Agriculture, and that regulatory oversight does not confer control over its business decisions.
GMA News Online has reached out to Montemayor for comment. The story will be updated once a response is received. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3-billion security breach
articles.summary: An initial investigation suggests the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers

blocks.text: BINANCE. Representations of cryptocurrencies are seen in front of displayed Binance logo in this illustration taken November 10, 2022.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
An initial investigation suggests the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers

items: Binance experienced a significant security breach, estimated to impact $6.3 billion, potentially marking the largest crypto heist in history, prompting concerns among investors about the safety of digital assets.

The exchange has managed to freeze approximately $3 billion of the affected assets and stated it would cover all hacking losses, while temporarily suspending deposits and withdrawals for security checks.
The incident has led to immediate market reactions, with notable drops in Bitcoin and Ether prices, and has raised alarms about the increasing vulnerability of cryptocurrency exchanges to hacks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3=billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets.

Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, October 30.

Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
The incident could be the world’s biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts.
“It’s the biggest hack in history,” said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic OTC business.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.

“User funds remain safe,” Binance said in a statement. “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
“It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them,” said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.
“My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.”
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance’s Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.

Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown actor.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.

In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders. – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP now on full alert for Undas 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) has placed all its units nationwide on full alert status starting Friday as authorities prepare for expected influx of people visiting cemeteries and traveling…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 12:06pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) has placed all its units nationwide on full alert status starting Friday as authorities prepare for expected influx of people visiting cemeteries and traveling during Undas 2026.
PNP Deputy Chief for Administration Lieutenant General Wilson Lopez said around 141,000 personnel from the PNP and augmentation forces have been deployed to secure the occasion.
“Kaninang madaling araw (Early morning), all PNP units nationwide are placed on full alert status from today up to November 3,” Lopez said at a press briefing.
“A total of approximately 141,000 personnel from the PNP and other augment forces. Our force multipliers have been deployed to ensure a safe, peaceful and orderly observance of the Undas,” he added.
In Metro Manila, National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) chief Police Brigadier General Christopher Abrahano said around 25,000 personnel would be available.
Of this number, around 7,000 personnel will be deployed to priority areas, including cemeteries, roads and transportation hubs.
Abrahano said police are also monitoring residential areas and commercial establishments to prevent crimes such as burglaries while residents are away visiting their departed loved ones.

“Ang focus natin, hindi lang doon sa sementeryo, dapat sa kanilang bahay, considered yun. Yung pupuntahan nila, pagkatapos ng pagpunta nila sa sementeryo, yung restaurants, babantayan din yun. Basically, it's a holistic approach,” he said.

(Our focus is not just on the cemetery, it should also be on their homes, that's considered. Where they go, after they go to the cemetery, the restaurants, that will also be monitored. Basically, it's a holistic approach.)
The NCRPO recorded approximately 1.8 million cemetery visitors during Undas last year.
As of the latest report on Friday, more than 1,000 people had already visited the Manila North Cemetery.
Abrahano said regular police patrols, crime prevention activities, and anti-criminality operations would continue alongside the Undas security deployment.
Authorities urged the public to remain vigilant and cooperate with authorities to ensure a peaceful observance of Undas 2026. —VAL, GMA News

Profile
2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardee Tommy Koh spent his lifetime shaping the youth, upholding peaceful coexistence, and preserving Singapore’s heritage
By Lourence Angelo Marcellana | Published October 30, 2026
Tommy Koh is Singapore’s youngest and oldest ambassador, who entered foreign service in 1968 and served as a permanent representative to the United Nations (UN).
Before, other diplomats mistook him for the ambassador’s son. But he used his age to his advantage and asked the seniors to mentor him.
And that’s how his career began.

For 55 years, Koh has been at the center of Singapore’s peace talks, business meetings, and negotiations with other countries. It’s a daunting task; every decision he makes carries the weight of the nation’s future. This has been the 88-year-old diplomat’s life.

In August, that chapter closed. But his influence on the youth, justice, and national heritage extends beyond his retirement. In the same month, Koh was named one of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award recipients — the fourth in his country to receive the Asian equivalent of the Nobel Prize.
The statesman was recognized for his leadership in international diplomacy and for shaping a new generation of advocates devoted to justice and human dignity around the world.
COLLEAGUES. Tommy Koh along with his colleagues at National University of Singapore Tembusu College. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

Koh was the founding chairman of the National University of Singapore’s (NUS) Centre for International Law in 2009, and the founding rector of NUS Tembusu College in 2011 — one of the four residential colleges in the university that were the first of their kind in Singapore and Southeast Asia.
He believes he was born to love and seek peace. For him, it has been the foundation of his illustrious career.
Early influences

In his early years, Koh loved reading. His father had a library of books and magazines, but he was also allowed to buy more books at a bookstore. His mother, who was an actress and dancer, exposed him to culture and the arts.

World War II marked his childhood when Singapore fell under Japanese occupation for three years. During that time, the Japanese army tried to purge pro-British and anti-Japanese Singaporeans from the country. Some passed the screening, while others suffered a fate far worse.
Years later, at just 12 years old, he made his first international trip to Kuala Lumpur. Koh was among those selected to represent Singapore’s Boy Scouts at the World Scout Jamboree.

In college, he pursued a Bachelor of Laws at NUS. As a student, he regularly listened to the BBC World Service on the radio and read publications of the Royal Institute of International Affairs (Chatham House), an independent policy institute.
He later obtained his master’s degree in law from Harvard University in 1964, and a postgraduate degree in criminology from Cambridge University in 1965.
The ‘Great Negotiator’

In 2014, Harvard Law School hailed Koh as one of the “Great Negotiators,” a recognition given to individuals whose lifetime achievements in high-stakes negotiation and dispute resolution have left a lasting impact on society.

DINNER. Tommy Koh spends his dinner with his mentor and the first Asian president of the United Nations General Assembly, Carlos P. Romulo, and his wife, Beth Day. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

But early in his career, Koh described himself as “young and ignorant” — that is, until his time with the UN, where he was mentored by former Philippine foreign secretary and UN General Assembly president Carlos Romulo.
He considers Romulo one of his “most important mentors.” Koh recalled that Romulo taught him how the UN works and what the proper diplomatic practices were.

“General Romulo, who had been president of the General Assembly, befriended me and mentored me. And I will always be grateful to him and to his wife, Beth Day,” Koh said in an online press interview last September 3.
He also looks up to Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, who led India’s independence from British colonial rule. But Koh took to heart the lessons Romulo taught him.

The diplomat represented his country and the UN on international law, environmental policy, trade, and disputes. From 1981 to 1982, he served as president of the Third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea or UNCLOS, helping establish a framework for the equitable and peaceful use of the world’s oceans.

FINAL ACT. Tommy Koh signs the final act of the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea, in December 1982, in Montego Bay, Jamaica. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

From 1990 to 1992, he chaired multiple committees for the Rio “Earth Summit,” the UN Conference on Environment and Development, which established the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change or UNFCCC in 1992. He also served as Singapore’s chief negotiator in free trade agreement talks with the United States.
A FRIEND. Tommy Koh accompanies former president of Indonesia, Suharto, at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

Among his successful negotiations was siding with Cambodia in 1979. He led the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) diplomatic delegation to the UN after the country was invaded by Vietnam in the same year. Koh opposed the crimes committed by Vietnam under the Khmer Rouge, which included the Ba Chúc Massacre, where over 3,000 civilians were slain.

He took part in negotiations, rejecting the legitimacy of the puppet government and criticizing it as foreign intervention and a violation of international law. In 1991, the Paris Conference recognized Cambodia’s sovereignty, independence, and neutral status.

“Even though you’re small, you must defend your rights and not allow the big country to bully you. You must have the courage to hold big countries to account when they violate the law and the UN Charter.”
Tommy Koh

He also represented Singapore in formal negotiations with China for the first time in 1990, when tensions arose because of military agreements with Taiwan. After going back and forth thrice, Singapore and China found common ground and established diplomatic ties. Today, Koh said that China is the country’s biggest trading partner.

HONOR. Tommy Koh receives the Order of San Nila Utama, Singapore’s third most prestigious national honor, from former Singapore president S. R. Nathan, in 2008. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

He helped resolve the dispute between Russia and Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia after the Cold War, and the decade-long territorial dispute between Singapore and Malaysia. He also assisted in the formation of the ASEAN Charter.
According to Koh, Southeast Asian countries are willing to take disputes to international arbitration, citing the West Philippine Sea case.

“If we are not successful, we take it to a binding third-party procedure. So, one of our disputes with Malaysia was solved in the International Court of Justice. Another one went to arbitration, and Malaysia took us to Italy. And eventually we settled by amicable agreement,” said Koh.

“That’s our story. And that is really ASEAN’s story. When they dispute with one another, and they can’t be solved by negotiation, we are willing to take them to arbitration, to a court of law. And it’s a very good thing.”
The art of ‘give and take’

Negotiations are always a process of “give and take,” according to Koh. They should be fair and balanced to all sides, he said, adding that each side must be willing to recognize and accommodate the other’s interests.
He jokingly compared it to a husband-and-wife relationship in terms of compromises — only in this case, the wife is always right.
Even when countries conflict, dialogue must always happen. He said there should be a fine line between human and work relations despite the differences.
CHAIR. Tommy Koh serving as chairman of the Preparatory Committee for the Earth Summit in New York in April 1992. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

During the Cambodian-Vietnamese War, ASEAN condemned Vietnam’s invasion. At the time, India sided with Vietnam. Yet despite the conflict, Koh had a strong relationship with India’s former national security advisor, Brajesh Mishra. He considers Mishra his older brother and guru, a spiritual mentor. His ASEAN friends scolded him for it.

When asked why he is still friends with Mishra, he replied: “He had been good to me in the past, and I will always be grateful to him. We may disagree today, but don’t personalize the disagreement. Disagreement is between India and Singapore, not between Brajesh and me.”
During disputes in foreign diplomacy, his advice is not to take them personally and to keep the human connection — which is bigger than their roles as negotiators — alive.
The blueprint of hope
Poverty, inequality, and backwardness are inevitable in any society, Koh said. He said that unemployment was high in Singapore when it gained independence.

Solving these problems is not impossible as long as social responsibility is a part of everyday life. He said Singapore’s growth from an underdeveloped country to one of the world’s richest cities can be attributed to four things — a blueprint for every nation: eradicating corruption, upholding meritocracy, promoting racial and religious harmony, and building a good education system.
“What unites Singapore as a nation is not just birth; it is a belief in a set of values.”

IN CONVERSATION. Tommy Koh sits down to chair a talk by former Singapore prime minister Lee Kuan Yew to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the Singapore Botanic Gardens in 2009. Photo courtesy of Tommy Koh/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation
Koh said Singapore stands on these four pillars, mindful of choosing its leaders who share the same vision.
“People vote not on the basis of race but on the basis of merit…. We need politicians who are not just self-seeking, but really interested in working for the people,” said Koh.

Singapore is also known for its diverse cultures and races, stemming from its historical roots as an international trading hub. Koh emphasized the importance of historical preservation through museums and monuments.
Monuments and markers make Singaporeans feel they belong in the country, the founding chairman of the National Arts Council said. It extends not just to preservation efforts, but also to practice.

Despite his retirement, Koh has never stopped. He continues to pass down the lessons he’s learned throughout his career to the next generation at NUS. His roles may have changed, but — if his latest award is any indication — his influence endures. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: PNP now on full alert for Undas 2026

The Philippine National Police (PNP) has placed all its units nationwide on full alert status starting Friday as authorities prepare for expected influx of people visiting cemeteries and traveling during Undas 2026.
PNP Deputy Chief for Administration Lieutenant General Wilson Lopez said around 141,000 personnel from the PNP and augmentation forces have been deployed to secure the occasion.
“Kaninang madaling araw (Early morning), all PNP units nationwide are placed on full alert status from today up to November 3,” Lopez said at a press briefing.
“A total of approximately 141,000 personnel from the PNP and other augment forces. Our force multipliers have been deployed to ensure a safe, peaceful and orderly observance of the Undas,” he added.
Marcos assures gov't readiness for 'safe, orderly' Undas 2026 exodus

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said the government is making the necessary preparations to ensure the safe and orderly trip for Filipinos who will head to their respective provinces or travel elsewhere for this year’s Undas.

In a video message, the President said the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and its attached agencies are now conducting extensive and thorough inspections at airports, seaports, and bus terminals to guarantee the safety of passengers.
He said urgent repairs on roads would also be completed by October 29 to minimize traffic woes during the surge in travel.
The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB), meanwhile, issued over a thousand special permits for additional buses to ensure sufficient public transport for passengers.

Marcos said the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) would also issue a relaxation order and special permits from October 29 to November 3, to allow a more flexible travel schedule for passenger vessels. Additional trips will also be provided on certain routes if necessary.
For those traveling in or out of the country, the President also assured the public that all immigration counters would remain fully staffed from October 30 to November 3.

“Nais nating tiyakin na magiging ligtas, maayos, at maginhawa ang kanilang pagbiyahe at pagdalaw. Pinaghahandaan na ng pamahalaan ang iba't ibang pangangailangan ng ating mga kababayan para sa Undas,” Marcos said.
(We want to ensure that their travel and visit will be safe, orderly, and comfortable. The government is already preparing for the various needs of our countrymen for Undas.)
“Kasabay ng pagdagsa ng mga pasahero, magkakaroon ng round-the-clock help desk ang mga pangunahing terminal mula 29 Oktober hanggang 3 November upang umalalay sa mga biyahero,” he added.
(As passengers flock to terminals, major transport hubs will have round-the-clock help desks from October 29 to November 3 to assist travelers.)
In Metro Manila, the President said that over 2,000 personnel of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) would be deployed to help manage traffic, particularly in areas near cemeteries.
PH braces for Undas 2026 rush
Government agencies have intensified preparations for the expected influx of passengers traveling to their home provinces for Undas 2026.
Interviewed on GMA News’ Unang Balita Friday, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said they have been conducting inspections at bus terminals to ensure the safety of passengers.
“Ang kabilin-bilinan po ng Pangulo na ligtas at kumbinyente ang biyahe ng mga kababayan natin lalo na ngayong long weekend ng Undas,” Dizon said.
He said authorities have been conducting driver assessments and roadworthiness inspections of public utility vehicles. Several drivers and vehicles were apprehended for violations.
Meanwhile, Philippine Ports Authority (PPA) spokesperson Eunice Samonte said passenger traffic at major ports remained manageable as of Friday morning.
“Wala pa pong gaanong kahabang mga pila. Tuloy-tuloy pa rin po ang ating mga operasyon and wala pa po tayong naitala na mga fully-booked but lahat po may mabo-book pa silang mga biyahe,” she said.
Around 200,000 passengers were recorded on Thursday, which was lower compared to previous records, Samonte said.
Around 1.93 million passengers are expected during the Undas period or 1.55% higher than last year's figure, according to the PPA official.

articles.title: PNP: Bato dela Rosa still in PH, manhunt intensifies
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Friday its manhunt for Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa would be intensified following the expiration of the deadline for his voluntary surrender.

blocks.text: SURRENDER DEADLINE ENDS
Published October 30, 2026 11:48am
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Friday its manhunt for Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa would be intensified following the expiration of the deadline for his voluntary surrender.

PNP Deputy Chief for Administration Lieutenant General Wilson Lopez, supervisor of the manhunt for Dela Rosa, said the senator remains in the Philippines, based on the Bureau of Immigration's (BI) update.
"Let me declare, hindi tayo uurong sa ating tungkulin," he said at a press briefing.
(Let me declare, we will not back down from our duty.)

"Ang PNP hindi tumigil sa paghahanap kay Senator Dela Rosa. Ang kaibahan lang this time ay mas magiging intensified 'yung operations nating gagawin. We'll be exerting full effort. At sabi ko nga, we have assigned specific task groups to do the purpose," he added.

(The PNP has not stopped searching for Senator Dela Rosa. The only difference is that this time the operations we will carry out will be more intensified. We'll be exerting full effort. And as I said, we have assigned specific task groups to do the purpose.)
Lopez said the police organization has reorganized its tracker teams and established dedicated task groups at the national and regional levels to locate Dela Rosa.
The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) earlier gave an ultimatum for Dela Rosa and urged him to surrender within one week.
Bounty
Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla earlier announced a P50-million reward for information leading to Dela Rosa's arrest.

According to Lopez, the PNP has received numerous calls through hotlines opened for the public to provide information on Dela Rosa's whereabouts. However, all information received was still undergoing validation.
Lopez also said the police have not received any feelers regarding Dela Rosa's possible voluntary surrender.
The PNP official said authorities are considering Dela Rosa's possible escape routes including backdoor exits as part of its operations.

Asked if the PNP is ready for a possible encounter with Dela Rosa during the manhunt, Lopez said, "In all operations, we are always considering all angles. So lahat ng possible things na puwede nangyari, kino-consider po natin and that's part of the plan."
(In all operations, we are always considering all angles. So all possible things that could happen, we are considering and that's part of the plan.)
Hunting the former PNP chief
Lopez expressed hope that Dela Rosa would not allow any police officer to get hurt in the manhunt operation as the senator was a former PNP chief.

"Kung titignan natin, si Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa ay dating magulang, dating tatay ng PNP. Kung sa puso niya ay naroon pa ang pagiging tatay ng PNP at kung hindi niya hahayaan na mayroong isa o dalawa o any members of the PNP na masaktan," Lopez said.

(If we look at it, Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa is a former parent, a former father of the PNP. If in his heart there is still being a father of the PNP and if he will not let one or two or any members of the PNP get hurt.)
Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes perpetrated during Duterte's war on drugs.
Earlier, the DILG claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao under the protection of an "armed and powerful group," but did not identify the organization. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: New York police will now investigate Cornell sex complaints, governor says
articles.summary: The change was announced amid backlash over the school's handling of gang rape allegations involving a fraternity on campus.

blocks.text: Hochul said New York State Police signed an agreement with Cornell University so that all sexual offence complaints, which had historically fallen under the jurisdiction of university police, will be immediately referred to state police instead.

"When someone reports sexual assault," Hochul said on Thursday, they deserve "to know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors".
"Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them," the governor added.
Backlash against the Ivy League university has been intense since Jane Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September.

On Wednesday, the institution's Faculty Senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff, met behind closed-doors and decided to move forward with voting on a resolution of no-confidence against the administration and the university's President Michael Kotlikoff.
The vote will be open for faculty starting on Friday and run until 6 November. The vote is largely symbolic but could intensify pressure on changing the university's leadership.
Earlier this month, the university announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including adding sexual assault investigators to its police force.

Hochul had said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, earlier this month to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.
The woman at the centre of the case filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.

articles.title: Tiangco bares details of House-approved ₱2.2-B proposed budget for Navotas
articles.summary: At least P2.28 billion of infrastructure projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) have been allocated to the lone district of Navotas under the House-approved P7.2 trillion…

blocks.text: 'FOR TRANSPARENCY'
Published October 30, 2026 11:31am

At least P2.28 billion of infrastructure projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) have been allocated to the lone district of Navotas under the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed national budget for 2027, Navotas Rep. Tobias Tiangco said.

Tiangco made the disclosure in a Facebook live, saying that this is is his way of being transparent on which projects he wants funded for the benefit of his constituents following consultations with DPWH officials and the City Engineering Office.
The P2.28 billion is broken down to:

items: P1.609 billion worth of projects approved by the Regional Development Council and civil society organizations for Navotas worth as provided under the DPWH’s proposed budget under the National Expenditure Program and
P673 million worth additional DPWH-proposed projects that was added by the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: The P2.28 billion, Tiangco said, covers 39 projects.
"Kung ayaw nilang gawing mandatory ang transparency, sisimulan ko sa sarili kong distrito. Walang dahilan para itago sa taumbayan kung saan napupunta ang kanilangpera," Tiangco said.
(If they don’t want to make transparency mandatory, I will start on my districts. There’s no reason for the public to wonder where their taxes are being spent on.)
Tiangco then urged his colleagues to follow his cue by voluntarily disclosing their respective district allocations and projects.

"Kung kaya nating ipakita sa mga taga-Navotas kung magkano ang budget, saan ito gagamitin, at bakit ito ang mga proyektong pinili, sana ganito rin ang gawin ng lahat ng kongresista. Karapatan ng bawat Pilipino na malamankung paano ginagastos ang kanilang pera," he said.
(If I can show how much is the budget and its purpose, there’s no reason for the rest of us to do the same. It is the right of the Filipinos to know where public funds are spent.)
"Hindi puwedeng transparency lang kapag budget ng ibang ahensya ang pinag-uusapan. Dapat magsimula mismo sa amin sa Kongreso. Ang budget ay pera ng taumbayan, hindi ng mga politiko," he stressed.
(We cannot just stand for transparency when just talking about a specific agency.)
Transparency, Tiangco said, is not an option for public officials.
"Transparency should be the standard for everyone in government. And that standard must begin with us," Tiangco said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Feral deer will become Australia’s next feral pig problem without prompt action, report warns
articles.summary:
The invasive species has increased in spread and numbers and is costing farmers millions of dollars

  • Get our

blocks.text: An unpublished government report on feral deer shows Australia is failing in its efforts to stop the spread of what one advocate warns could become “Australia’s next feral pig”.

The five years from 2020-2025 over which the national feral deer action plan was assessed covers a period in which the famously elusive species has increasingly encroached upon major cities, leading to more frequent encounters – including a memorable occasion in which two men in various degrees of undress were fined after becoming lost in the bush when they were spooked by deer while nude sunbathing.

The report says deer, one of the country’s “most rapidly increasing invasive pests”, have both increased in numbers and spread in territory, costing more than $91m in production loss and management time every year.
Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie, president of the Australian Mammal Society, said he was “not at all” surprised by this year’s national vertebrate pest management report card.

“This report shows that governments are failing miserably to invest enough to control deer populations and the severe impacts that they can have on agriculture, native wildlife and the environment, road safety and culturally significant sites,” Ritchie said.
“This is what sustained failure to act sufficiently results in.”

Six species of feral deer are established in Australia – chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa and sambar – with well-established populations across south-eastern Australia, where densities are highest. There are smaller, more localised populations in South and Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

The report card, produced by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, shows every state and territory is failing or floundering in their efforts to control feral deer – with one notable exception. South Australia, which launched an ambitious statewide eradication plan in 2022, received a green in all four categories assessed under the traffic light system of marking. The report showed – with high confidence – that the state had decreased the abundance, distribution and environmental and agricultural impacts of deer.
New South Wales and Tasmania were given reds in all four categories, while Queensland and the ACT both received three reds and a yellow. No jurisdiction but SA received a single green pass mark.

Invasive Species Council advocacy manager Reece Pianta said the report confirmed what land managers had been seeing on the ground for some years. In May 2025, the council released footage and images that it said showed the Gold Coast “under feral deer siege”.

Pianta said the report, leaked to his organisation, points to “a long-term systemic underfunding of deer control”. He said deer did not have the recognition of other more notorious invasives, but controlling them was every bit as necessary.
“Deer are the next feral pig,” he said. “The difference with deer is that an intervention now could make a significant difference to the population numbers and contain, or even reverse, that spread.”
after newsletter promotion

While Pianta said deer “probably can’t be eradicated” from the entire continent, he said South Australia’s “A+” report score showed it was possible to do so in some states and territories, while others would require a long-term effort to contain the spread of deer and mitigate their impacts.
Adelaide University Environment Institute director Prof Andrew Lowe said the report was a “good news story” for his state that rang true with what he was seeing on the ground.

Lowe, who is also member of the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, which is involved in managing deer, said SA grappled with its “massive problem with deer” in earnest from 2022, after an agricultural impact estimate showed the $36m worth of damage done every year by deer there was set to increase to $241m by 2031.

But although deer had “massively declined” in the few years since a $4m eradication program began, Lowe said deer were seeking refuge on the fringes of urban areas, where culling was more expensive. He said functional eradication of deer from SA would take about another $10m over 10 years.
The cost of inaction, though, was of a different magnitude.
“If we don’t do that, then the population will go up again and we’re going to be in the same situation,” Lowe said. “So $10m versus $240m – do the math.”

articles.title: Marcos assures gov't readiness for 'safe, orderly' Undas 2026 exodus
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said the government is making the necessary preparations to ensure the safe and orderly trip for Filipinos who will head to their respective…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 11:18am

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said the government is making the necessary preparations to ensure the safe and orderly trip for Filipinos who will head to their respective provinces or travel elsewhere for this year’s Undas.

In a video message, the President said the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and its attached agencies are now conducting extensive and thorough inspections at airports, seaports, and bus terminals to guarantee the safety of passengers.
He said urgent repairs on roads would also be completed by October 29 to minimize traffic woes during the surge in travel.
The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB), meanwhile, issued over a thousand special permits for additional buses to ensure sufficient public transport for passengers.

Marcos said the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) would also issue a relaxation order and special permits from October 29 to November 3, to allow a more flexible travel schedule for passenger vessels. Additional trips will also be provided on certain routes if necessary.
For those traveling in or out of the country, the President also assured the public that all immigration counters would remain fully staffed from October 30 to November 3.

“Nais nating tiyakin na magiging ligtas, maayos, at maginhawa ang kanilang pagbiyahe at pagdalaw. Pinaghahandaan na ng pamahalaan ang iba't ibang pangangailangan ng ating mga kababayan para sa Undas,” Marcos said.
(We want to ensure that their travel and visit will be safe, orderly, and comfortable. The government is already preparing for the various needs of our countrymen for Undas.)
“Kasabay ng pagdagsa ng mga pasahero, magkakaroon ng round-the-clock help desk ang mga pangunahing terminal mula 29 Oktober hanggang 3 November upang umalalay sa mga biyahero,” he added.
(As passengers flock to terminals, major transport hubs will have round-the-clock help desks from October 29 to November 3 to assist travelers.)
In Metro Manila, the President said that over 2,000 personnel of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) would be deployed to help manage traffic, particularly in areas near cemeteries.

Marcos said various agencies are also conducting inspections to ensure safety in cemeteries, churches, and other crowded areas. Police officers would also be deployed in these areas to maintain order.
Hospitals and health emergency teams are on standby in case of emergencies, according to the President.
He also advised people who will be traveling to plan their trips well, and stay informed for traffic advisories and possible route changes.

“Kung gagamit ng pampublikong transportasyon, agahan ang pagpunta sa terminal. Kung maaari, bumili na ng tiket nang maaga. Para sa mga biyaheng may online ticketing, hinihikayat natin kayong gamitin ito upang makaiwas sa mahahabang pila sa mga terminal,” Marcos said.

(If you are taking public transportation, arrive at the terminal early. If possible, purchase your tickets in advance. For trips that offer online ticketing, we encourage you to use this option to avoid long queues at the terminals.)
“Mag-ingat din sa pagdadala at pagsisindi ng kandila. Sundin ang mga patakaran sa sementeryo at makipagtulungan sa ating mga awtoridad. At higit sa lahat, mag-ingat sa inyong paglalakbay,” he added.
(Exercise caution when bringing or lighting candles. Follow the rules at the cemetery and cooperate with our authorities. And above all, stay safe during your travels.)
The President also emphasized that the 911 hotline is available for times of emergencies, and the official social media pages of concerned agencies are ready to disseminate timely information.
“Ang Undas ay panahon ng paggunita at pag-alala sa ating mga mahal sa buhay. Nawa’y maging payapa at makabuluhan ang pagdalaw ng bawat pamilyang Pilipino,” Marcos said.
(Undas is a time for commemoration and remembering our departed loved ones. May the visit of every Filipino family be peaceful and meaningful.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado says US backs 2027 election
articles.summary: The return of Maria Corina Machado, who says Trump opened the "floodgate to freedom" for Venezuela, presents a challenge for Washington as Trump has also backed interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

image.caption: Machado reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners [FILE: October 28, 2026]Image: Federico Parra/AFP

blocks.text: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.

Calling the transition to democracy "irreversible," Machado said, "US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes ​presidential elections in 2027."
"The date of the election is the date of liberation," Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.

Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
Shortly before Machado's public statements, Rodriguez announced that there "will be elections" in Venezuela, without specifying a date.
Machado says Trump helped open 'floodgate to freedom'
Machado, who famously "presented" US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to "the floodgate to freedom" being opened in Venezuela.
The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.
"This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," she said.

At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.
US caught in a bind

Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.
Machado's recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.
